lines.text: by opening their eyes to the invisible reality which is veiled
by the visible. The visible situation is their abandonment and
distress. What is the invisible reality which stands behind
that visible scene? Their triumphant ascendancy over the
hostile world. For what invisibly takes place in the unfolding
of those terrible visible events of the crucifixion of Jesus and
the persecution of the Church, is in truth nothing other than
the judgment of the world. "And when He comes He will
convince the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of
judgment." What is the meaning of this?
The title which in the Johannine farewell discourses is
given to the Spirit has the meaning of helper and advocate;
in fact what is really meant is an advocate in a judgment
scene. And this is basically the meaning of the remarkable
verse: the Spirit discloses to the mind the truth that the
events which Jesus and His own experience constitute are
in fact the great judgment before the judgment seat of God,
in which the Spirit is their advocate. What is here in question
is the divine judgment which will not first take place at the
end of time, but which is even now being enacted; it is the
divine judgment on the world.
The Spirit opens the eyes to this truth; for the world it
remains hidden and that is the terrible thing, that the world
itself does not know that its judgment is continually taking
place.
How does this come about? The poet says: "World
history implies world judgment." But this is not the meaning
here. For the poet wishes to affirm that in the course of world
history all wrong is avenged, all right finally triumphs, and
that the development of world history is an upward progress
towards the light. But the gospel does not suggest this. For
the Christian faith (and not it alone) knows, or can know,
that this belief is an illusion, and that the struggle between
right and wrong, between truth and falsehood in world
history is never decisively closed, but lasts as long as earth
remains. Savagery that had apparently been mastered breaks
out afresh one day; crimes of wanton wickedness, the like of
